subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: At the tea stall in Nagaur, Harish stood shoulder to shoulder with Deepak, talking the way people do in a small town where everyone stands close. It reminded Harish of the internship in Stuttgart. There, Harish had stood a hand's width from a colleague, chatting eagerly, and the colleague had taken one step back, then another. Harish felt rejected and wondered what had been said wrong. Weeks later a co-intern explained that some people there like a wider gap, and that it was comfort, not dislike. "So I started noticing," Harish told Deepak, "who leans in and who steps away." Harish moved half a step back, just to try. Deepak laughed and stepped in closer, and they both grinned.

qa.q: Where did Harish's internship take place?
qa.a: The internship was in Stuttgart.

qa.q: How did Harish feel when the colleague stepped back?
qa.a: Rejected and confused, wondering what had been said wrong.

qa.q: What did Harish learn to do afterwards?
qa.a: Notice who leans in and who steps away, and adjust the distance.

qa.q: How might Deepak see Harish moving half a step back?
qa.a: As a funny experiment, since Deepak laughed and stepped in closer.

grounding: A young adult who stood close to a colleague abroad felt rejected, then learned about different comfort distances.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: On her third day at the design studio in Helsinki, Aiko leaned in beside Xin to look at a drawing, close enough to smell the tea. Xin took a small step back. Aiko stepped forward again. Xin stepped back again, and Aiko's cheeks went hot. Rejected, Aiko ate lunch alone and wondered what had gone wrong. That afternoon a note from the placement guide mentioned that people differ in how much space feels comfortable. Aiko asked Xin, "Am I standing too close?" Xin smiled. "A little. It's not about you, I just like room." After that Aiko kept an arm's length, and Xin began to lean in first when sharing sketches.

qa.q: What did Xin do when Aiko leaned in?
qa.a: Xin took a small step back.

qa.q: How did Aiko feel at lunch, and why?
qa.a: Rejected and confused; Aiko's cheeks had gone hot and Aiko ate alone wondering what had gone wrong.

qa.q: What did Aiko do that turned it around?
qa.a: Asked Xin openly whether Aiko was standing too close, then kept an arm's length.

qa.q: What is it like for Xin when someone stands very close?
qa.a: Uncomfortable, since Xin likes room, but Xin says it is not about Aiko personally.

grounding: A young adult standing close sees a colleague step back, feels rejected, and learns about different comfort distances.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage:
Wednesday, Stockholm, 11 pm
Third week at the internship. Today at the coffee machine I was explaining my data slides to Erik, standing the way I'd stand with anyone in the Pune office, maybe an arm's length. He took a step back. I stepped forward, to keep talking. He stepped back again, into the bin. I felt my cheeks go hot. I thought, he doesn't like me, or I smell of the hostel's dal.
At lunch I sat alone and replayed it. Then Rajni, the senior analyst who moved here from Chennai years ago, sat with me and asked what was wrong. She laughed, gently. "People here like more space. Watch where they stand in the queue." I watched. There are gaps between everyone, even friends.
Tomorrow I'll stand a bit further back and see if Erik stops stepping. Indu, the space cadet.

qa.q: Where did Indu stand while explaining the slides to Erik?
qa.a: At the coffee machine, maybe an arm's length away, the way Indu would stand in the Pune office.

qa.q: How did Indu feel when Erik kept stepping back?
qa.a: Indu felt embarrassed and rejected, cheeks hot, and worried that Erik disliked Indu.

qa.q: What did Rajni suggest, and why is it useful?
qa.a: She suggested watching where people stand in the queue, which lets Indu read local comfort distance and adjust.

qa.q: How might Erik have experienced the conversation at the coffee machine?
qa.a: Erik probably felt crowded and uncomfortable, not unfriendly, and kept stepping back to get the space he was used to.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult abroad who stands close to a colleague, feels rejected when they step back, and later learns about different comfort distances.

passage:
Parul: darshan are u awake
Darshan: always. what happened
Parul: my team lead here stepped away from me TWICE today
Parul: I was just showing her my screen. she moved her chair back like I had a cold
Darshan: maybe you did have a cold 😅
Parul: not funny. I felt like a creep. I've been miserable all evening
Darshan: ok ok. what did the others do?
Parul: actually... everyone sits far apart. at lunch there's like a gap between every tray
Darshan: so maybe it's not you. maybe it's Tokyo
Parul: hmm. Megumi from HR told me people here keep more space, I thought it was just her
Darshan: try tomorrow. put your laptop between you and turn the screen. see what she does
Parul: ok
Parul: update: she leaned IN to see the screen 🙂 and said thank you
Darshan: see. space cadet 🚀

qa.q: What did the team lead do when Parul showed her the screen?
qa.a: She moved her chair back.

qa.q: How did Parul feel after the team lead moved away?
qa.a: Parul felt rejected and ashamed, like a creep, and was miserable all evening.

qa.q: What did Darshan suggest, and why did it work?
qa.a: To put the laptop between them and turn the screen, which gave the team lead her comfortable space so she could lean in by choice.

qa.q: How might the team lead have seen Parul sitting close?
qa.a: She probably felt crowded and a little uneasy, and moved back for comfort rather than out of dislike.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult abroad who sits close to a colleague, feels rejected when they move away, and learns about different comfort distances.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage:
The dairy co-operative in Moga had a visitor that month: Anouk, an agriculture trainer from the Netherlands, who worked alongside the staff. Alka, twenty, was chosen to translate for her. On the first morning, walking between the milk cans, Alka stood right at her shoulder, the way she and the other girls always stood, close enough to smell the tea. Anouk kept stepping sideways. By noon Alka felt hurt and foolish. Did she smell of cattle? Did she talk too much? She went quiet.
In the afternoon, Amandeep, the co-op supervisor, pulled her aside. "Her people keep a bigger gap. My cousin in Canada says the same about everyone there." Alka watched Anouk with the farmers after that: she kept about a stride away from all of them. The next day Alka stood a stride away too. Anouk smiled, and they talked for an hour.

qa.q: How far away did Anouk stand from the farmers?
qa.a: About a stride away.

qa.q: How did Alka feel by noon on the first day?
qa.a: Alka felt hurt and foolish, worrying she smelled of cattle or talked too much, and went quiet.

qa.q: What did Alka do that shows courtesy across cultures?
qa.a: She watched how Anouk stood with others, then adjusted her own distance to a stride, which let Anouk feel comfortable.

qa.q: How might Anouk have experienced the first morning?
qa.a: Anouk probably felt crowded and kept stepping sideways for comfort, perhaps without realising Alka felt rejected.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who stands close to a colleague from abroad, sees her step back and feels rejected, then learns about comfort distances and adjusts.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: In his first week at the lab in Copenhagen, Javier stood beside Ines at the coffee machine the way he would have in Bogota, shoulders almost touching, chatting warmly about the experiment. Ines took a step back. He stepped in again to keep talking. She stepped back again, until she was against the counter. That evening Javier sat in his flat feeling rejected. Maybe she didn't like him, or didn't like Colombians. On Friday the lab manager, Sofie, ran a short welcome session for new international staff and mentioned, between bike rules and lunch times, that people here often stand about an arm's length apart. Javier went red. On Monday at the machine he kept an arm's length. Ines talked for twenty minutes, asked about his family and invited him to Thursday's board-game night.

qa.q: How far apart did Sofie say people here often stand?
qa.a: About an arm's length apart.

qa.q: What did Javier feel that evening in his flat?
qa.a: Javier felt rejected and unsure, wondering whether Ines disliked him or Colombians.

qa.q: What basic courtesy did Javier learn to use?
qa.a: Noticing body language like stepping back, and adjusting his distance to local comfort, as he did on Monday.

qa.q: Why might Ines have kept stepping back?
qa.a: Ines was probably just uncomfortable with how close he stood, not rejecting him, as her warm talk on Monday shows.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult abroad who stands close to a colleague, feels rejected when she steps back, and later learns about different comfort distances and adjusts.
